title: Run game paves way for Monmouth's dominant first-ever win over UNH - Asbury Park Press
content: How did Monmouth's run game contribute to their victory? What defensive plays helped Monmouth secure the win? Why did Monmouth's physical approach lead to their first win over UNH? It's one thing to break down a longstanding barrier, it's another bulldoze right through it. Monmouth football did the latter on Saturday afternoon in Durham, N.H. For four straight years, the Hawks had lost to New Hampshire since joining the Coastal Athletic Association in 2022. They made sure that the fifth opportunity would erase any lingering memories of those past disappointments. Monmouth went on the road and dominated the Wildcats for four quarters, getting their first-ever victory over New Hampshire in a 42-21 rout to improve to 5-2 and remain unbeaten in conference play. "On the road, winning a CAA game is huge," Monmouth head coach Jeff Gallo said. "It's about this team, this year, and our opportunity to come get this game and make a point. It's for our former players who played these games and lost some tough ones to them. And I felt good going into it. We fought all the way through. We started fast, we out-physicaled them, and we took control of the game." The final score would be enough of a testament to the team's dominant effort, but the manner in which the win unfolded further reflected the emphatic showing by the Hawks. FCS No. 20 Monmouth ran the ball 62 times for 326 yards and four touchdowns. Both Kenny Smith Jr. (175) and Elijah Jennings (126) surpassed the century mark on the day on what was easily the team's most prolific ground performance of the season. The Hawks raced out of the gates and never looked back. After forcing a three-and-out, Monmouth ran the ball with Jennings on the first six plays of the game before the seventh was a 2-yard touchdown run by former Keyport standout Nazir Treadwell, who added 22 more rushing yards to the impressive total. After another UNH three-and-out, the Hawks' second drive of the game was the start of a career day for Smith, as five of the seven plays were runs to the redshirt freshman including the 6-yard touchdown to finish it and give Monmouth a 14-0 lead midway through the first quarter. "We wanted to come up here and be the more physical team, the more energized team," Gallo said. "To be able to run the ball into the wind and find some throws with the wind at our back. And I think just the o-line and running backs, we set the tone." The Hawks were also the beneficiaries of several New Hampshire lapses that combined with difficult windy conditions to put the Wildcats in an early hole. There were several drops, offset by many overthrows, as the UNH offense couldn't get anything going in the first half. To further exasperate the situation for the home team, swirling winds undermined any attempts by either team to punt. That was less of an issue for Monmouth, who started in opposing territory on four of their first six drives and each of those resulted in a touchdown. Monmouth seized on New Hampshire's struggles and capitalized on every opportunity. The strong run game set up a play action pass from quarterback Frankie Weaver to Tra Neal for 35-yard touchdown to extend the lead to 21-0 after the first quarter. Weaver finished the day 16-for-25 for 195 yards and two touchdowns with no interceptions, while Neal had a team-high 82 receiving yards on five catches. After the offense stalled slightly on the two next possessions, the Hawks finished the half strong by going back to the run game. The wide-open running lanes were cleared by upperclassmen that had experienced the years of struggles against New Hampshire, like senior center Kevin Shriner, guard Michael Petito, and tight end Shane Garrett, all of whom got to enjoy the catharsis of a physically-dominating effort upfront. For Garrett, that effort was appropriately rewarded with a play action touchdown pass from Weaver to close out the first half with a 28-0 lead. It was the first career touchdown reception for the redshirt junior from Ocean Township. "He's a program kid. He works his butt off. He's everything you want in a player," Gallo "Shore kid, great family, son of a coach. He comes to work every day and he does all the dirty work. And when we throw it to him, he's gonna catch it." New Hampshire's offensive challenges were exacerbated by the Monmouth defense, and the Wildcats decided to make quarterback change after starter Brooks Bentley was just 3-for-11 for 29 yards at halftime. That did appear to slightly spark the Wildcats momentarily, as they opened the second half by forcing a three-and-out and then running back Myles Thomason, a former Seton Hall Prep standout, authored a two-play drive with 44 rushing yards and a touchdown. But that would be the only glimmer of hope for New Hampshire. The Hawks answered with a nine-play, 75-yard drive that culminated with a 27-yard touchdown by Smith. The Hawks carried a 35-7 lead until the final five minutes, when both teams added late points with the game already decided. Those seven points allowed until garbage time are strong testament to the Monmouth defense, which took advantage of the New Hampshire mistakes and created plenty of negative plays on their own. Ryan Russo had a crucial forced fumble that set up the Hawks' touchdown before halftime. Mounir Keshen and JJ Lewis both contributed sacks, an impressive showing for two front four players that are also reliable run defenders. And a third down pressure by Jahide Lesaine resulted in an interception by Jaeden Jones in the third quarter. The win is quite the milestone for the Hawks. It's obviously always a breakthrough to get a first-ever win against a conference opponent, but it was also encouraging that there was no lag in the team's performance coming out of the bye week. Furthermore, it was their first game since Monmouth rejoined the FCS top 25 two weeks ago. They'll likely see another rankings bump after the decisive victory. More importantly, the Hawks continue to sit atop the CAA standings as the only 4-0 team in conference play. Monmouth got a big boost from Albany on Saturday, as the Great Danes knocked off rival Stony Brook 48-31. The Seawolves were the only other remaining unbeaten in the CAA that Monmouth doesn't play this season, and their loss means the Hawks control their own destiny to a conference title. No. 18 Campbell (6-1, 3-0) and Bryant (5-2, 3-0) are the other remaining unbeaten teams in league play. Monmouth will be on the road next Saturday against 1-6 Hampton and will need to not look past that game even as a Halloween showdown at home against Bryant looms. "Focus on what matters, and that's playing your best football," Gallo said. "Was it our best football? No. We can play better. We played relatively well, but there's room for improvement. And now we focus on the next one at Hampton and we're gonna bring the same mentality. It's a road game in the CAA. It's their homecoming. It's a great opportunity for us and a great challenge. The rankings don't matter to me, it's more about how we play." Obviously a recurring theme for the Hawks is one-week seasons and that will need to continue to avoid any let downs before the key matchup against Bryant in two weeks. But for this week's season, finally beating New Hampshire carried a bit more weight and thusly, a bit more cathartic relief. "We were aware that we hadn't beaten them, but it was about this team, this year, this game," Gallo said. "We came out and really got after it, which was great to see. And it's great for our alumni, it's great for our university, it's great for our fans. It's a good program win." With the wild winds limiting the options in the passing game to create offensive balance, the Hawks became more dynamic in the run game with a wide variety of designs and formations to keep the New Hampshire defense off-balance. The periphery movement and unique formations were clever disguises for a rushing attack that also deployed several counter punches in addition to straightforward dominance at the line of scrimmage. The first two touchdowns epitomized what worked so well for the Monmouth offense on Saturday. On the first score, Nazir Treadwell came out in a variation of the usual goal line wildcat formation, which was tweaked to sub out the quarterback for an extra blocker. Tra Neal motioned in for a chip on the left side, creating enough space for G/H power (guard and h-back pulling) to clear the way to the end zone. The second score was a more conventional variation of a similar concept. This time the Hawks came out in a pistol unbalanced formation and motioned Gavin Nelson to be the chip blocker and again they pulled the left guard Collin Goetter on power. But instead of a second puller, the "H" element was in insert block from tight end Marcus Middleton, paving the way for Kenny Smith on the 6-yard touchdown. In the second quarter, the Hawks used an even bolder design to spark an explosive run play. Monmouth initially came out in an ace set with two slot receivers to the left, motioned tight end to the right for a twins set, and then pulled center Kevin Shriner and guard Reed Collins on a what appeared to be a buck sweep to the short side of the field. The look allowed Smith to turn the corner for a 33-yard gain. The play actions looks were more conventional, although the last touchdown of the first half to Shane Garrett was interesting. Garrett lined up in the slot and then motioned across to give the appearance of split zone, but he raced to the flat in what appeared to be a lower red zone run-pass option for Frankie Weaver as opposed to straight play action. And the third layer to the various designs helped put the game out of reach. The Hawks got their first touchdown of the second half on a really fascinating run design. The Hawks came out with trips to the left and Smith also aligned to the left of Weaver, a de facto quads set to the short side of the field. The lone receiver to the right, Keshawn Mister, moved backwards across the formation to give a reverse look, which cleared the space for the play's true intent: a G/H sweep with Goetter and Middleton pulling to clear the way for Smith's 27-yard touchdown. What is very cool about that play is that it is a Wing-T concept in principle with the misdirection, but executed out of a traditional spread formation. With an additional bye week to prepare and the motivation to beat New Hampshire for the first time, the Hawks brought out some of their best run designs in the win. There were some intriguing defensive fronts, particularly on third down, that the Monmouth defense used to stifle a New Hampshire offense that also shot itself in the foot. But instead of focusing on the X's and the O's, it's time to highlight some Jimmys and Joes that are emerging for the Hawks. JJ Lewis has to be at the top of the list. The senior joined Monmouth last year as a transfer from D-II Findlay, and he has come into his own this fall. In addition to his sack, he recovered Russo's first fumble that led to the key score before halftime. He is second on the team with three sacks and also has two pass break ups. His ability to be a disruptive presence on the interior is a huge boost for the front four as a whole, as the interior is usually shaped by stalwart run defenders. Lewis has shown the ability to do both. Complimenting him on the edge is Mounir Keshen, who continues his ascent as a premier defender, and Hunter Watson. So much of Monmouth's sack production last year was on third down in clear passing situations, but Watson and Keshen have emerged as premier rushers on early downs in addition to being stout against the run. Keshen leads the team with 3.5 sacks while Watson also has three. The growth of the trio of Watson, Keshen and Lewis has the potential to be a game-changer for the Hawks down the stretch. With limited angles on the broadcast of a road game, it's challenging to assess exactly what's happening in the secondary. The Hawks continue to use a deep rotation of players with varying results, as positive flashes can also be offset by maddening lapses. But the bright spot continues to be the safeties. Jaeden Jones is of course a star, but Donovan Fey had several excellent moments against UNH. He seemed to recognize a potential coverage breakdown in pre-snap, and recovered to the seam for a key pass breakup in the first half. He can be a nightmare for opposing receivers, delivering punishing hits while attacking the catch point to separate his man from the ball. Aside from some late coverage lapses and two runs by Myles Thomason that went for 44 yards and a score, this was a lights-out performance from the Monmouth defense. The Hawks will look to build on it next week against Hampton. We may earn a commission when you buy through links on this page. title: David Ismail ends scoring drought, leads Vermont soccer to comeback win over UNH - Yahoo Sports
content: David Ismail ended a two-month scoring drought and Vermont soccer prolonged a yearslong home unbeaten streak typical Catamount fashion: A second-half comeback with a late-regulation winner. Ismail, who scored for the first time since Aug. 23 with a first-half penalty strike, blasted in the go-ahead goal in the 84th minute, capping Vermont's rally for a 3-2 victory over New Hampshire in front of 2,197 at windy Virtue Field on Saturday, Oct. 17. No. 16 Vermont (9-1-3, 3-0-1), which trailed 2-1 at the break, also extended its regular-season home unbeaten run to 27 consecutive games (19-0-8), a streak that started on Oct. 27, 2023. "Love the guys' response. What a great second-half attitude and what a way to turn the tide … and never give up," said Vermont first-year head coach Adrian Dubois, who is an UNH alum. "That is what Vermont football is. When you do that, good things are going to happen." DAVID ISMAIL WITH THE BRACE IN THE 84TH MINUTE 🚨🚨Vermont takes a 3-2 lead! Halim Bangura and Luis Vetter each tally an assist on UVM's third goal 😼#LetsRally pic.twitter.com/q4nCl1fPUD After Vermont was rewarded a PK following an officials' video review, Ismail converted from the spot in the 10th minute for a 1-0 lead. But the Catamounts, challenged by the windy conditions on defense, conceded a pair of goals in the 24th and 32nd minute, respectively. On the first UNH goal, Laurin Preuss supplied a pretty flick via Ryo Myata's corner kick that slipped under the bar to level the game. Then David Dravila rolled a shot past Vermont goalie Niklas Herceg (four saves), a goal that was initially ruled offside before another review overturned the call. In the second half, Ismail had two door-step chances with headers — the first smacked off the cross bar, the second UNH goalie Aaron Choi (five saves) snatched above his head. But in the 70th minute, the Catamounts found the equalizer via Philipp Schmidtke's fifth goal of 2026. A failed UNH clearance in the box fell to Schmidtke, who uncorked a lefty blast inside the left post. On the winner, Ismail uncorked a lefty rocket into the back of the net with authority for the 84th-minute winner, also his fifth goal this fall. "He's a top player. He's going to find a way. I'm just happy for him because he's the hardest worker on the team," Dubois said of Ismail. "That's going to give him a boost of energy and we need our best guys playing well right now. He had a really good game overall." Vermont travels to Albany for its next game on Saturday, Oct. 24. Contact Alex Abrami at aabrami@freepressmedia.com. title: Wrong-way crash on I-91 in North Haven leaves 1 dead, several injured - WFSB
content:
NORTH HAVEN, Conn. (WFSB) - A multi-vehicle crash caused by a wrong-way driver on I-91 southbound in North Haven left one person dead on Friday night. Troopers were called to the area of I-91 south near Exit 9 at around 11:43 p.m. after reports of a wrong-way driver where the vehicle was then involved in a multi-vehicle crash, according to state police. EMS and fire department personnel also responded to the scene, and the Connecticut Department of Transportation assisted with road closures. A man driving a Honda Accord was heading southbound on I-91 in the left lane while a man driving a pick up truck was traveling the wrong-way and struck his car in a head-on collision. The man who’s vehicle was struck then entered the left-center lane, where it was struck by another vehicle, a Jeep. The man then entered the right lane and right shoulder, where it was struck by a GMC SUV, state police said. State Police have identified the driver of the Honda Accord that was struck as 21-year-old Ryan O’Shea from Stony Point, New York. The University of New Haven confirmed that he was a criminal justice major with a concentration in police science at the school. He interned last summer with the New York City Police Department, where he hoped to start his career as a police officer after commencement. He was also a senior captain of the university’s club hockey team. O’Shea suffered fatal injuries in the crash and died on scene. The driver of the GMC SUV was transported to a nearby hospital with serious injuries. Also, the driver and the front passenger who were in the Jeep were suffered minor injuries and were transported to a local hospital as well as the driver of the GMC. The State Police Collision Analysis and Reconstruction Squad responded to the scene and is assisting with the investigation. State Police said this remains under active investigation. title: UNH Stock Rises Overnight Ahead Of Earnings: Analyst Outlines ‘Short Premium’ Play To Cut January Call Cost By Nearly 60% - Stocktwits
content: UnitedHealth (UNH) is set to report third-quarter (Q3) earnings before Tuesday’s market open, with options pricing in a 6.5% move around the results. Tidal Financial Group strategist Michael Khouw says elevated options prices create an opportunity for traders to sell November premium to help finance a cheaper January call. UNH stock rose 0.9% in after-hours trading on Monday after closing the regular session down 0.2% at $378.52. “The only thing more expensive than health insurance is perhaps the costs of insuring shares of health insurers,” Khouw said, pointing to UnitedHealth as an example. Options imply a 6.5% move in UnitedHealth shares around earnings, while implied volatility is running at about 40%, about twice the stock’s realized volatility of 20%, he said. The implied move is the second-largest in almost two years. Shares have fallen after five of their past eight earnings reports, including nearly 20% drops after results in January and April 2025, CNBC noted. Khouw’s proposed trade is a “short premium” strategy: It sells two November options to collect $10.60 per share and offset part of the cost of a longer-dated call. The trade buys a January 2027 $400 call for $18.20 per share, then sells a November $420 call for $5.80 and a November $340 put for $4.80. The resulting net cost is $7.60 per share, or $760 per contract, reducing the call’s upfront cost by about 58%. If UnitedHealth finishes November between $340 and $420: The short options would expire worthless. The January call’s breakeven would be $407.60 at expiration. If UNH stock falls below $340: The short put could require the seller to buy shares at that price, for an effective cost of about $347.60 per share after the trade’s net debit. Khouw said UnitedHealth had been essentially flat over five years and traded 12% to 13% below the midpoint of its two-year high-low range. At about 17 times forward earnings, he said, the stock was not priced for a recovery. He sees the company’s 13% to 16% earnings-growth target as achievable, though rising healthcare costs is a headwind. Khouw also pointed to enrollment trends. Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace enrollment appears poised to decline, he said, although the segment is smaller than Medicare and commercial coverage. Commercial fee-based enrollment grew about 2.9% from 2024 to 2025, while total Medicare enrollment rose 4.5%. Commercial growth exceeded U.S. workforce growth of about 1.4%. Koyfin’s estimates for the upcoming quarter compare with the last reported quarter. They show revenue of $111.49 billion, down 0.5% sequentially. Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) is estimated at $6.47 billion, down 28%, while earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) is forecast at $5.44 billion, down 32%. GAAP earnings per share (EPS) are projected to fall 36.81%. Fiscal.ai’s year-over-year estimates show revenue of $112.4 billion, compared with $113.2 billion a year earlier. It forecasts EBITDA of $6.45 billion, up from $5.25 billion, and earnings per share of $3.06, compared with $2.92. TD Cowen lowered its price target on UNH to $402 from $430, implying a 6% upside, while maintaining a 'Buy' rating. The firm expects preliminary commentary on 2027 earnings-per-share expectations with the report. Meanwhile, Piper Sandler said 66.8% of UnitedHealth members were enrolled in plans rated four stars or higher, based on September 2026 enrollment data, and called the company’s resilience “impressive” and underappreciated. Oppenheimer noted that the share of members in four-star-or-higher plans fell 15% at UnitedHealth for 2027, versus 10% at Elevance Health, 15% at CVS Health and 9% at Centene. Humana moved in the opposite direction, with 95% of its members in four-star-or-higher plans, up from 42% a year earlier. However, retail traders remain bearish on both stocks, highlighting investor concerns that recent rallies may have already priced in future growth. Both Nokia and BlackBerry stocks traded over 1% lower overnight, ahead of Tuesday. “Mad Money” host Jim Cramer pointed to Nokia’s push into artificial intelligence infrastructure. “They are doing AI fiber at the edge, which is really good,” he said. He also highlighted Nokia’s relationship with Nvidia Corp. (NVDA). “Don’t forget they took some money from Nvidia. I think they are actually a core component in the growth of the data center. It is very real.” Nokia has spent years trying to shed its image as a legacy telecom equipment maker. Cramer’s remarks cast it as a supplier to the AI data center buildout, the theme that has driven some of the market’s biggest moves. Cramer was just as upbeat on BlackBerry, a company that has reinvented itself from smartphone pioneer to software provider. “I like BlackBerry very much. I thought they had a very good story to tell. Shares of Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX) edged up on Monday even as Chinese memory-chip advances pressured sector stocks, with CEO Elon Musk weighing in on China’s manufacturing scale and calling SpaceX an “anomaly in the matrix.” SPCX stock rose 0.5% on Monday, marking its second straight gain after ending the previous week 2.3% higher. Micron fell 4% on Monday, while other memory and storage companies, including SK Hynix, Samsung, SanDisk, Seagate and Western Digital, also declined after Chinese chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) outlined plans for a new DDR5 server-memory product. CXMT said it aims to launch a server memory module using a “4F square” DRAM design by the end of the year. The architecture aims to pack more memory cells into the same chip area as the 6F square design widely used today, potentially increasing density. Musk contrasted China’s manufacturing scale on X with SpaceX’s launch lead. “When China figures out how to manufacture a product, their ability to scale is often greater than the rest of the world combined,” he said, citing lithium batteries and solar. He said SpaceX is a “rare counter-example”: it puts an order of magnitude more mass into orbit than the rest of the world, although China now accounts for most non-SpaceX mass to orbit. “SpaceX is an anomaly in the matrix,” he added. Musk then turned to memory chips, noting that RAM was a “low margin commodity” only about three years ago. He said LPDDR5 and LPDDR6 share a common standard that China “seems to be solving fast,” while newer high-bandwidth memory architectures, an SRAM layer beneath logic, 3D-stacked RAM above logic and the challenge of cooling the logic will be “harder to solve.” Musk’s comments follow SpaceX’s August earnings call, when he said memory supply was struggling to keep pace with AI-driven demand. He said memory output was growing about 20% a year while demand was increasing 200% or more, a gap he said could push prices higher. The supply issue matters to SpaceX’s expansion into AI computing, alongside its launch and Starlink businesses. Under a multi-year Google cloud-services agreement disclosed in June, Google is set to pay SpaceX $920 million a month from October 2026 through June 2029 for access to computing capacity, including about 110,000 Nvidia GPUs and related infrastructure with memory. The company reported $15.8 billion in AI-related capital expenditures, within about $18.4 billion in total capital expenditures. Revenue reached $7.8 billion, while SpaceX recorded a $541 million net loss. Musk is also pursuing a longer-term chip-supply strategy through Terafab, a Texas facility to make, package and test logic and memory chips. Intel joined the project in April, with its 14A manufacturing process expected to be used at the fab. In August, SpaceX and Tesla announced an initial $16.8 billion investment in the project. Musk also said recently that TSMC could potentially sublease part of the facility, while Tesla and SpaceX would retain ownership. content: Shares of UnitedHealth Group, Inc. (UNH) are headed for their fourth monthly win as Wall Street turns more bullish after a large second-quarter (Q2) earnings beat and a sweeping increase to its 2026 outlook. UNH stock rose 1% on Friday, bringing its monthly gain to nearly 3%, while shares also finished the week marginally higher. BofA called UnitedHealth’s quarter “impressive,” noting that earnings beat consensus by 31% and guidance rose 12%. The firm raised its price target to $512, implying over 20% upside, while reiterating a ‘Buy’ rating and citing a “strong” quarter and broad-based outlook increase. Morgan Stanley was even more bullish, lifting its target to $529, implying a 24% upside. The firm said the Q2 beat and higher 2026 targets “validate its disciplined strategy and establish a stronger base for future growth.” Truist, Oppenheimer and KeyBanc each moved to $500 targets, implying a 17% upside. Truist highlighted top- and bottom-line beats, a better Medical Care Ratio, and improving expectations for UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health. Oppenheimer said that the company “handily” topped expectations, while KeyBanc said results “topped bullish expectations” and argued UnitedHealth could hit $30 in earnings per share (EPS) sooner than anticipated. Goldman Sachs and UBS both raised their targets to $490, implying a 15% upside. Goldman cited a “material” earnings beat, stronger Optum Health profitability and a larger-than-expected guidance increase. UBS said UnitedHealth was “making good progress with more to go.” Meanwhile, RBC Capital raised its target to $478, implying a 12% upside. It remained positive on the earnings beat and guidance hike but flagged investor concern around persistent commercial medical-cost pressure. UnitedHealth posted adjusted EPS of $6.38, beating the $4.92 consensus and rising from $4.08 a year ago. Revenue of $112.03 billion also topped estimates, while the medical care ratio improved to 86.7% from 89.4%. Additionally, the company raised its 2026 adjusted EPS outlook to $19.50-$20 from more than $18.25, lifted UnitedHealthcare’s operating profit forecast to at least $12 billion, and increased Optum Health’s outlook to at least $2.2 billion. CEO Stephen Hemsley said UnitedHealth was “returning to form” as stronger performance disciplines took hold. He reaffirmed the company’s 13%-16% long-term earnings-growth target and doubled the 2026 buyback goal to at least $5 billion. Medicare Advantage drove the beat, with costs coming in below expectations. “Medicare delivered a strong second quarter,” UnitedHealthcare CEO Tim Noel said. Commercial plans remained the weak spot, with medical-cost trends above 11%. On the other hand, Optum said its tools added nearly 200,000 patient-facing hours, cut clinician cognitive burnout by 90%, and achieved a 96% first-pass approval rate for digital prior authorizations. ARK Investment Management founder-CEO Cathie Wood cheered Eli Lilly’s $3.8 billion AtaiBeckley acquisition on Sunday, calling it a “well-deserved” payoff for shareholders and a validation of Christian Angermayer’s psychedelic vision. ATAI stock rose 1% on Friday, adding 40% over the past five sessions and marking its best week in more than a year. Shares, however, were dipping more than 1% in overnight trading heading into Monday. Wood highlighted on X the biotech company’s role in bringing psychedelic medicines closer to mainstream clinical use: “Not only a well-deserved return for ATAI shareholders, this transaction validates Christian’s heartfelt mission and vision,” Wood said. She called Angermayer’s work with ATAI “one of the biggest catalysts of the psychedelic renaissance,” adding that clinical trials are increasingly validating the potential of psychedelics in treatment-resistant depression, post-traumatic stress disorder and broader mental health conditions. Wood also credited Angermayer with backing the field long before psychedelic medicine became widely accepted, fashionable, or investable. “Long before psychedelics were accepted, fashionable, or investable, Christian’s life’s mission was to reactivate them and bring back hope and health for those who had lost both,” she said. Wood’s praise came after ARK Invest reduced its ATAI stake last week. The ARK Genomic Revolution ETF (ARKG) sold 1.12 million ATAI shares worth about $6.02 million. As of Friday, however, ARKG still held 3.19 million shares valued at $22.78 million, or 1.4% of the fund. Lilly was also ARKG’s seventh-largest holding, with 61,258 shares worth $71.62 million and a 4.4% weighting. Eli Lilly said last week that it would acquire AtaiBeckley for up to $3.8 billion for the psychedelic drug developer as it builds out its neuroscience pipeline. Under the deal, shareholders would receive $6.75 in cash per ATAI share, with Lilly committing $2.8 billion at closing and an additional $1 billion for future milestones. The deal marked a 26% premium to AtaiBeckley’s shareholders. The companies are targeting completion of the acquisition in the third quarter of 2026. The centerpiece of the deal is BPL-003, an intranasal psychedelic therapy being tested in late-stage studies for treatment-resistant depression. Jefferies has projected that the drug could eventually generate $1 billion to $2 billion in sales if the program succeeds. AtaiBeckley has said the first late-stage data are expected in early 2029. Angermayer reflected on the deal over the weekend in an X post, saying ATAI’s next phase is about commercialization rather than advocacy. “Ten years ago, psychedelics needed an evangelist. Today, they need commercialization,” he said. After first exploring psychedelics in 2014, Angermayer helped launch Compass Pathways and ATAI in 2017 and invested more than $100 million of his own capital in ATAI. The two companies later raised over $1.5 billion, went public and helped build clinical credibility for psychedelic medicine. content: Shares of Apple Inc. (AAPL), AtaiBeckley Inc. (ATAI), and UnitedHealth Group Inc. (UNH) jumped to 52-week highs on Thursday amid company-specific triggers, Wall Street optimism, and strong earnings results. AAPL stock closed up nearly 2% higher on Thursday as Apple Intelligence AI service registration in China, alongside Wall Street optimism over the company’s recent strength, bolstered prices. ATAI stock jumped more than 33% at close after Eli Lilly (LLY) confirmed that it is acquiring the clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company. Meanwhile, UNH stock gained more than 1% after its second-quarter (Q2) earnings blew past Wall Street estimates and it also raised its full-year profit outlook. Shares of the iPhone maker clocked an all-time high of $334.68 on Thursday amid a series of positive catalysts for the company. China's cyberspace regulator on Wednesday approved the registration of Apple Intelligence for use on iPhones in the country, clearing a key regulatory hurdle for the long-awaited launch of Apple's AI features in the country. Under Chinese rules, companies must obtain approval for large language models and generative AI services before releasing them to the public. Apple Intelligence is expected to leverage AI models from Baidu and Alibaba. Meanwhile, HSBC upgraded AAPL stock to ‘Buy’ from ‘Hold,’ with a price target of $366, implying an upside of 10% from the stock’s last close. Apple has drawn increased attention in recent weeks after it announced hikes in prices for several products, including MacBooks, iPads, HomePods and Apple TV devices, fueling speculation that iPhone price increases could follow. Investors are also focused on the company's upcoming leadership change, with John Ternus set to succeed Tim Cook as CEO on Sept. 1. AAPL stock has risen nearly 23% so far in 2026, while retail sentiment on Stocktwits was ‘bullish’ at the time of writing. Shares of the psychedelics company surged to a yearly high of $7.22 after pharma giant Eli Lilly (LLY) confirmed its acquisition of AtaiBeckley. Eli Lilly said that it will acquire all outstanding ATAI shares for $6.75 per share in cash, with shareholders eligible for an additional up to $2.50 per share if certain development and regulatory milestones are achieved, bringing the deal's total potential value to $9.25 per share. The cash offer represents a 25.9% premium to ATAI's Wednesday closing price, while the maximum consideration implies a 72.6% premium. The acquisition is expected to close in the third quarter (Q3) of this year. ATAI stock is up more than 84% this year. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment was in the ‘extremely bullish’ territory at the time of writing. UNH stock touched a 52-week high of $461.62 in Thursday’s trading session after its second-quarter (Q2) earnings results blew past Wall Street estimates. The company posted revenue of $112.03 billion, up about 0.37% from $111.62 billion in the prior-year quarter. However, it beat Wall Street expectations of $110.9 billion, as per Fiscal.ai estimates. Meanwhile, net income came in at $5.48 billion, or $6.04 per share, compared with $3.41 billion, or $3.74 per share, in the same period a year ago. The health insurer now expects 2026 adjusted earnings of $19.50 to $20 per share, up from its prior outlook of more than $18.25 per share, while maintaining its revenue guidance of more than $439 billion for the year. The company attributed the better-than-expected results and higher full-year profit outlook to improved management of elevated medical costs and greater use of AI to streamline operations. UNH stock has gained nearly 26% so far in 2026, as retail sentiment improved from ‘bullish’ to ‘extremely bullish’ over 24 hours. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Shares of AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) suffered their worst one-day drop in more than two years on Thursday after a $1 billion convertible-note raise rattled investors, but options veteran Jon Najarian said that the deal still represents “a pretty strong bet to the upside.” ASTS stock plunged 17% on Thursday to close at $55.01, marking its lowest closing level of the year. Najarian and his brother Pete Najarian broke down the financing and ASTS’ selloff in a Market Rebellion video posted on X. The brothers co-founded Market Rebellion, an options-focused market analysis platform, in 2016. AST SpaceMobile priced $1 billion of 1.625% convertible senior notes due in 2034, with an initial conversion price of $79.57 per share, which was about 20% above Wednesday’s close. Jon Najarian said that the notes give buyers the right, but not the obligation, to convert into ASTS shares at that price. While the 1.625% coupon is relatively low, he said the real appeal lies in the potential equity upside. “If the stock’s 200 bucks, you’re still exercising it at $79.57,” he said, calling the structure “a pretty strong bet to the upside.” The $200 figure was a hypothetical example, not a formal price target. Pete Najarian said that investors were focused on the risk that the notes could eventually convert into shares and dilute existing holders. “They’re concerned about dilution and all the rest of it,” he said, adding that the stock’s negative reaction was “understandable.” Still, he agreed the financing could support a valuable long-term opportunity. “I think this could be something into the future that could be pretty special, quite frankly,” he said. The brothers also stressed that ASTS remains a highly volatile trade. Implied volatility in the options was around 100%, according to Pete Najarian. “The implied volatility of this thing is not a joke,” he said. “Hell yes, this thing is volatile.” AST SpaceMobile said proceeds remaining after capped-call transactions may be used to secure additional access to orbit through “partnerships and/or acquisitions.” The company said the move could further vertically integrate its business and reduce reliance on third-party launch providers, although it currently has no agreement for any transaction. Satellite communications analyst Tim Farrar said that the language pointed to a potential acquisition. Potential names raised included United Launch Alliance, Firefly Aerospace, Relativity Space and Stoke Space. Farrar also said that AST may be trying to copy Rocket Lab’s vertically integrated model across launch and satellite infrastructure. “ASTS were outbid for Iridium, so it looks like they are now trying to copy Rocket Lab’s vertical integration play,” he said. The Najarians also suggested acquisitions may be part of the plan. “They’ve got some ideas with partnerships, acquisitions, all that kind of thing that people are excited about,” Jon Najarian said. “They just needed the capital,” he added. The financing comes as AST SpaceMobile continues expanding its BlueBird satellite network. BlueBird 10 recently deployed its communications array in low Earth orbit, while BlueBirds 8 and 9 are next. BlueBird 11 has arrived at Cape Canaveral, and BlueBirds 12 and 13 are being transported from Texas to Florida. AST said that the newer satellites are expected to deliver nearly twice the peak speeds of its first-generation spacecraft. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for ASTS slipped to ‘neutral’ from ‘bullish’ levels a day ago amid ‘high’ message volume. A Stocktwits poll with more than 2,000 votes showed retail traders largely remained bullish despite the selloff, with 49% saying they were "buying the dip," while 21% were waiting for a better entry, 19% planned to hold their positions, and just 11% said they were selling or trimming. The company said in a statement on Thursday that it will launch Truth API, a new business-to-business data feed, expected to become available to institutional customers from August 1. DJT has already signed up customers ahead of the launch and is onboarding additional partners in the weeks ahead, it said. With no official integrated API previously available, companies seeking to track key Truth Social posts had to monitor the platform manually. As adoption grows, we expect Truth API to become a meaningful, ongoing source of revenue for the company, creating lasting value for shareholders.” Virginia Canter, an ethics attorney with Democracy Defenders Fund, a nonprofit organization, told CNBC that this was a “huge” conflict of interest, adding that the president has an “obligation” to the American people to convey information to them publicly, and “he’s now funneling it through a private channel in which he has a private interest as one of its largest shareholders.” Meanwhile, CEO of Euro Pacific Asset Management Peter Schiff noted the development in an X post, saying “In the latest Trump grift, Truth Social will now sell faster access to Trump’s market-moving posts to institutional investors willing to pay for it. IBM (IBM), Oracle (ORCL), and NuScale Power (SMR) stocks dropped to fresh 52-week lows on Thursday amid fresh worries over whether the heavy AI-related investments would deliver sufficient financial returns, highlighting a broader shift in market sentiment, with investors placing greater emphasis on cash flow, margins and execution rather than long-term growth expectations. Oracle and NuScale Power stocks tumbled 6% and 8% respectively, while IBM stock pared losses to end the session 3% higher. IBM stock reached a new yearly low of $204.44, extending losses after the company acknowledged that it failed to adapt quickly enough to shifting customer demand. IBM’s comment that enterprise customers are prioritizing AI infrastructure investments, delaying or reducing spending on traditional software offerings, has added additional pressure. On Thursday, Argus analyst Jim Kelleher reduced his price target on IBM shares to $280 from $360 while reaffirming a ‘Buy’ rating, following IBM's negative pre-announcement for its fiscal second-quarter results, which indicated that key infrastructure revenue would fall short of earlier expectations. The firm added that while IBM had been monitoring higher component costs, particularly rising memory prices, the company underestimated the extent to which those market dynamics would influence customer buying behavior. IBM has declined 26% so far this year, with retail sentiment on Stocktwits remaining in ‘extremely bullish’ territory. Oracle stock tumbled to a fresh 52-week low of $123.66 on investors' concern about the company's aggressive investments in Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, which have resulted in elevated capital expenditures and negative free cash flow. Additional pressure came from concerns surrounding leverage and its credit profile, with S&P Global lowering the company’s credit rating to BBB- last week, only one level above non-investment-grade status. The agency highlighted concerns about Oracle’s reliance on large customers, including OpenAI, which represents a large portion of its remaining performance obligations. Despite those headwinds, Oracle has introduced financing initiatives, including allowing customers to deploy their own chips within Oracle data centers. The company is also competing for a major secure cloud contract with the Japanese government. Oracle has cratered 36% year-to-date, with sentiment around the stock remaining in ‘extremely bullish’ territory. The company raised its 2026 capex forecast to between $60 billion and $64 billion in its latest earnings update on Thursday, up substantially from its previous $52 billion to $56 billion range. content: UnitedHealth Group Incorporated UNH showed further signs of a turnaround in the third quarter of 2026, with stronger earnings and improving profitability.Earnings beat expectations, medical costs eased, and management raised its annual outlook again. UNH shares jumped 7.4% since then. However, declining membership raises questions about whether the company can sustain its earnings recovery over the long term. UNH reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $4.69 per share,beating the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $4.12 and rising 60.6% year over year.Revenues reached $112.7 billion, exceeding the consensus estimate by 1.2% but slipping from $113.2 billion last year. Operating earnings climbed to $6.6 billion from $4.3 billion, while net margin improved to 3.6% from 2.1%. The standout number was the medical care ratio, which measures the share of premium revenue spent on medical services. It fell to 88.4% from 89.9% a year ago. Even a modest improvement in this measure can have a large effect on earnings for an insurer of UnitedHealth's size. Lower claims pressure, tighter pricing and redesigned benefits helped drive the change. However, the quarter included $610 million of favorable medical reserve development related to 2026 care. Still, the operating cost ratio also improved to 12.8% from 13.5%, pointing to progress beyond claims alone. It again raised its 2026 adjusted earnings forecast to at least $20.50 per share from its previous $19.50-$20 range. For further details, see UNH Tops Q3 Earnings on Lower Medical Costs, Raises '26 Outlook. Are Better Margins Coming at the Expense of Growth? That is the central debate after earnings. UnitedHealthcare served 48.3 million people, down from 50.1 million a year ago. Medicare Advantage membership has fallen by 935,000 since the end of 2025 as the company withdrew from less attractive business and adjusted benefits. The financial payoff: UnitedHealthcare's operating profit increased to $2.8 billion from $1.8 billion despite lower revenue. Its operating margin climbed to 3.3% from 2.1%. Management now expects Medicare Advantage margins near the upper end of its 2-4% target range for 2026. Executives emphasized dual-eligible and chronic-condition plans alongside higher-value HMOs, rather than chasing enrollment across every product. More than 94% of Medicare-eligible Americans will have access to a UnitedHealthcare Medicare offering next year. A smaller, better-priced book seems healthier than growth that destroys profit. Still, a lasting turnaround requires enrollment to stabilize. Formal 2027 membership guidance remains ahead, making the upcoming selling season an important checkpoint. Optum offers another reason for optimism. Segment operating earnings rose to $3.7 billion from $2.5 billion even as revenue declined to $66.9 billion from $69.2 billion. Its margin expanded to 5.6% from 3.6%. Optum Health's turnaround was particularly notable. Operating earnings jumped to $735 million from just $41 million last year, with the margin reaching 3.2%. Revenue fell 10% as the business reduced exposure to markets where its value-based care operations lacked scale. Management expects further improvement in Optum Health's profitability in 2027 as it works toward its 6-8% margin target for 2028. Optum Insight's automation tools and Optum Rx's pharmacy operations offer additional earnings opportunities, but the company still must convert those initiatives into consistent growth. Optum Rx also faces pressure from lower prescription volumes tied to UnitedHealthcare's shrinking membership. Adjusted prescriptions declined to 393 million from 414 million. External customers now account for more than half its covered lives, however, reducing dependence on the insurance business. title: UNH Stock Outpaces S&P 500 In 2026, Eyes Best Year Since Pandemic — CFO Says Wall Street May Be Missing 2027 Upside - Stocktwits
content: Shares of UnitedHealth (UNH) have outpaced the S&P 500 so far in 2026 and are on pace for their strongest year since 2021. Now, CFO Wayne DeVeydt says Wall Street may be underestimating the company’s earnings opportunity in 2027. UNH stock is up nearly 17% in 2026, outpacing the S&P 500’s 14% gain and the Health Care Select Sector SPDR Fund’s (XLV) 11% rise. The rebound follows a 33% plunge last year. UnitedHealth reported third-quarter (Q3) adjusted earnings of $4.69 per share, topping the $4.14 analyst consensus. Revenue also beat estimates, coming in at $112.69 billion on $111.49 billion, though it was slightly below the $113.2 billion reported a year earlier. Earnings from operations climbed to $6.6 billion from $4.3 billion. The company raised its 2026 adjusted earnings outlook to at least $20.50 per share, from a previous range of $19.50 to $20. But even after its recent rebound, UNH shares are up just 19% since January 2021, a 3% annualized gain over nearly six years. “Current analyst consensus for 2027 may understate the opportunity ahead,” DeVeydt said on the earnings call. He added, “The quality of earnings is strong and durable as we head into 2027.” He called the lower end of UnitedHealth’s long-term adjusted earnings growth target of 13% to 16% a “reasonable starting point.” By Stocktwits’ calculation, 13% growth on the $20.50 floor would imply about $23.17 a share in 2027. Analysts’ quarterly estimates compiled by Fiscal.ai sum to about $22.80. DeVeydt cited share repurchases, value-based care, enterprise-wide progress and gains from artificial intelligence and modernization as potential tailwinds. He also flagged policy reforms, modernization spending, medical-cost trends and pressure on health-benefit funding as headwinds. Quarterly revenue climbed 61% from $70.2 billion in the first quarter of 2021 to $112.7 billion in the third quarter of 2026. Operating profit, however, was nearly unchanged, slipping from $6.7 billion to $6.6 billion. Revenue hovered around $112 billion in the second and third quarters of 2026, while earnings per share swung more sharply. Basic EPS fell to nearly zero in the fourth quarter of 2025, rebounded to $6.90 in the first quarter of 2026, then declined to $6.10 in the second quarter and $4.60 in the third. UnitedHealth reported adjusted EPS of $2.11 for the fourth quarter of 2025. Analysts estimate basic EPS will peak at $8.20 in the first quarter of 2027, then fall to $6.90 in the second quarter, $4.80 in the third and $2.90 in the fourth, according to Fiscal.ai. UnitedHealth’s average 12-month analyst price target is $480.68, implying about 27% upside from current levels. Of 26 analysts, 7 rate the stock ‘Strong Buy,’ 15 ‘Buy’ and 4 ‘Hold’; none rate it ‘Sell’ or ‘Strong Sell,’ according to Koyfin. UnitedHealth’s medical care ratio fell to 88.4% in the third quarter from 89.9% a year earlier, reflecting tighter pricing, benefit changes and cost controls. The result also included $610 million in favorable reserve development. But the ratio rose from 86.7% in the second quarter, and commercial medical trends remained above 11%. When asked whether the trends were worsening, UnitedHealthcare CEO Tim Noel said, “We are not seeing the dynamics that you are talking about.” Medicaid is another pressure point. UnitedHealth expects 2026 to be a trough year for core Medicaid margins, which it now projects to be moderately better than negative 1%. The firm expects margins to return to targeted levels by the end of 2028. At least 69% of UnitedHealthcare’s Medicare Advantage members are in plans rated four stars or higher in the 2027 star ratings, which affect bonus payments in 2028. The company expects that share to reach 75% as it moves through 2027 and into 2028, compared with a 70% industry average. The company plans to focus on high-value Health Maintenance Organization (HMO) plans and special-needs plans for people with chronic conditions or who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid. UnitedHealthcare is UnitedHealth’s revenue heavyweight, bringing in $86.3 billion in the third quarter. It provides health coverage to employers and individuals and runs the company’s Medicare Advantage and Medicaid plans. Revenue dipped from $87.1 billion a year earlier, but operating earnings climbed to $2.8 billion from $1.8 billion. Optum is the group’s health-services engine. Optum Health delivers care and manages provider networks. Optum Rx handles pharmacy services and prescription benefits. Optum Insight provides tech and data services to healthcare organizations. Together, the businesses generated $66.9 billion in revenue and $3.7 billion in operating earnings. Optum Health’s earnings surged to $735 million from $41 million, while Optum Rx said external clients made up more than half its membership for the first time. Retention remained in the high 90s. Shares of Rocket Lab (RKLB) climbed nearly 1% overnight late Tuesday after an executive said that the company is planning 12 hypersonic test launches this year, spotlighting its role in the U.S. push to develop advanced weapons faster. RKLB stock fell 2% on Tuesday to $64.22, logging its fifth straight session in the red. Rocket Lab’s vice president of global launch services Brian Rogers said that said HASTE enables “low cost, high frequency hypersonic and missile defense testing.” Short for Hypersonic Accelerator Suborbital Test Electron, HASTE is a suborbital test-launch vehicle derived from Rocket Lab’s Electron rocket. It carries experimental payloads for flight testing. Rocket Lab says it can carry payloads of up to 700 kilograms and release them at speeds above 7.5 kilometers per second. The company reported a 100% success rate across HASTE flights in March. “Rather than saying we need to be stuck in an analysis environment and then it’s a very rigorous test campaign that costs a lot of money and involves a lot of people, now you can say we’re planning 12 tests this year,” Rogers told Fox News. “We don’t have to bet the farm on any one of them, which allows us to take more risk and really move the needle in terms of technology development.” The U.S. military is replenishing its missile stockpile, while developing hypersonic weapons, but the systems are costly. Government Accountability Office estimates put the Army’s Dark Eagle missile at more than $40 million each. A Navy estimate for a hypersonic missile planned for Zumwalt destroyers is about $70 million, including development and integration costs. By comparison, a Tomahawk costs about $2.6 million and an Army Precision Strike Missile about $1.6 million. Some startups are targeting lower prices. In July, Rocket Lab announced a $266 million Space Force contract for 12 suborbital launches, with options for six more. The missions will primarily launch from a new site in Kodiak, Alaska, with the first expected no earlier than the end of 2026. title: New SAARA Bulletin on Supporting Siblings with Disabilities - University of New Hampshire
content: We are excited to share our latest SAARA Bulletin, "Preventing Sibling Aggression and Abuse for Children with Disabilities." In the U.S., one in six children has developmental or neurodevelopmental disabilities. While many children with disabilities have positive sibling relationships, some can face difficulties that increase their risk of harming or being harmed by their siblings. In families with children with disabilities, balancing different needs and navigating sibling relationships can be challenging. Learn how parents can foster healthy sibling relationships and build skills that help prevent sibling aggression and abuse. title: UNH, HUM, CNC Stocks Rally On Medicare Advantage Rate Surprise - Stocktwits
content: Shares of insurers UnitedHealth Group (UNH), Centene (CNC), Humana (HUM), and Elevance Health (ELV) jumped in Monday’s extended trading hours after the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced that the payments to private insurers offering Medicare Advantage plans will increase 2.48% next year. This increase implies $13 billion in additional payments to Medicare insurers for the year, the agency said. “When accounting for estimated risk score trend in MA due to factors such as population changes and coding practices, this amounts to a 4.98% increase,” the agency added. The move came as a surprise since in January, the CMS had proposed a roughly flat increase in payments for private Medicare plans the following year, sending shares of insurers down and wiping out about $100 billion in stock market value. The announcement further comes as a relief to the industry plagued by concerns over rising medical costs. Shares of UNH, CNC, HUM and ELV rallied between 5% and 11% at the time of writing. Shares of Aetna parent CVS Health (CVS) rose by about 6.5% while Molina Healthcare (MOH) stock rose a modest 3%. title: CNC, UNH, CVS, HUM Stocks Slip After-Hours — Trump Administration Reportedly Seeks To Scrap Subsidies On Certain Medicare Plans - Stocktwits
content: Shares of health insurance companies, including Centene (CNC), slipped after-hours on Tuesday following a report that the Trump administration plans to end a federal subsidy program that has helped suppress Medicare Part D prescription drug plan premiums. The federal program is currently channeling an estimated $3.6 billion to insurers this year to keep Part D premiums in check. Officials told The Wall Street Journal that the support will expire after 2026 and will not be extended into 2027. The Journal states that about 25 million Americans are enrolled in Part D plans, with the average monthly premium this year running near $36. The Wall Street Journal reports the decision could leave many seniors confronting higher premiums for their stand-alone prescription coverage beginning in 2027. Without the federal support, plan sponsors may pass increased costs to enrollees, potentially accelerating shifts toward Medicare Advantage plans that bundle drug benefits. An administration official quoted by the Journal projected that roughly one-quarter of Part D enrollees will see their premiums hold steady or decline in 2027, about 30% will face hikes under $10 a month, and the remaining 45% will largely see increases in the $11–$20 range. The subsidy primarily benefits insurers offering stand-alone Part D plans (PDPs). Companies with substantial PDP enrollment—UnitedHealth Group (UNH), CVS Health (CVS, via Aetna), Humana (HUM), Centene (CNC, via WellCare), and Molina Healthcare (MOH)—stand to lose this revenue stream. Loss of the $3.6-billion in support could pressure margins if insurers absorb costs or reduce competitiveness through higher premiums, risking enrollment declines. However, beneficiaries might also migrate to Medicare Advantage plans and help offset losses. Centene holds the largest share of stand-alone Medicare Part D (PDP) enrollment via Wellcare — more than eight million members as of early 2026, or about one-third of the entire PDP market, exceeding the exposure of its rivals. CNC shares dived 3% after hours on Tuesday, while shares of UNH, CVS, and HUM fell by about or less than 1%. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around CNC jumped from ‘bearish’ to ‘bullish’ territory over the past 24 hours, while message volume rose from ‘normal’ to ‘high’ levels. In a major bid to accelerate American dominance in the commercial space sector, the Trump administration announced a proposal allowing the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to bypass lengthy environmental reviews for rocket launches, spacecraft reentries, and commercial launch site approvals. The initiative, announced on Tuesday by Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy, aims to eliminate red tape for commercial operators as the U.S. prepares for an unprecedented surge in orbital launches and space infrastructure development. Commercial space stocks, including Rocket Lab (RKLB), AST SpaceMobile (ASTS), Intuitive Machines (LUNR), and Planet Labs (PL) dropped between 3% and 7% on Tuesday, while SpaceX (SPCX) added 3%. Under the proposed framework, the FAA would gain the authority to waive requirements established across 13 major federal environmental statutes. These include the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act, and the Clean Air Act. Federal officials emphasized that exemptions would only apply where environmental rules delay innovation, maintaining that core public health, national security, and safety safeguards will remain intact. "America won the first Space Race, and we can do it again -- but only if we get government red tape out of the way," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy stated, noting that the goal is to lower costs and strengthen U.S. competitiveness. Environmental assessments—which currently can take over a year to complete—have long been a target of frustration for commercial launch providers. While conservation groups view these evaluations as crucial for protecting coastal wildlife habitats, launch companies have repeatedly slammed the reviews as duplicative administrative bottlenecks. The FAA's proposal opens a 30-day public comment window before final rules are enacted. The drive to deregulate comes as the commercial space industry experiences exponential growth. The FAA reported authorizing a record 204 commercial space operations in FY2025. Over the next decade, federal forecasts project total operations could reach over 4,200, climbing from 214 this year to more than 500 annual operations by 2036. Much of this growth is being driven by heavyweights like Elon Musk’s SpaceX, Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, and rising startups like Stoke Space. These firms are aggressively deploying satellite constellations for broadband connectivity, defense applications, and orbital data centers. Rocket Lab (RKLB) made massive waves in the market after announcing an $8-billion acquisition of Iridium Communications. The deal hands Rocket Lab an operational 66-satellite network, global L-band spectrum, and 2.55 million active subscribers, firmly establishing it as the primary commercial competitor to SpaceX. AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) confirmed its next-generation BlueBird 8, 9, and 10 satellites are fully operational in orbit, while SpaceX recently cleared its FAA mishap investigation for Starship Flight 12, paving the way for Flight 13 as it prepares for up to 44 orbital launches annually from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Shares of Lucid Motors (LCID) jumped as much as 29% on Tuesday after Saudi billionaire Prince Alwaleed bin Talal acquired a 5% stake in the electric vehicle maker. At the time of writing, LCID stock pared some of the gains and was trading 23% higher. According to a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Tuesday, the prince now beneficially owns 19.5 million shares of Lucid’s Class A common stock. The stake equates to exactly 5% of the class, based on 390.26 million shares outstanding as of April 29, the filing showed. The prince’s spokesperson reportedly told Bloomberg that the purchases were made during a recent slump in LCID’s share price. Lucid, based in California, already maintains close links to Saudi Arabia through its majority shareholder, the Public Investment Fund. PIF holds a majority stake of around 57% in Lucid Group, according to a company filing from late April. The stake is held primarily through Ayar Third Investment Company, a wholly owned PIF subsidiary. Earlier this month, Lucid rejected reports that it was considering bankruptcy or a take-private transaction, noting that it has sufficient liquidity to carry its operations well into next year. The company also delivered a cease and desist letter to the publication that carried the bankruptcy rumors, stating that the company “unequivocally denies the central factual assertions” in the article. Lucid is now slated to provide a further update on its financials in its second-quarter earnings call scheduled for August 4. The company, however, has faced significant headwinds. Earlier this month, the company reported second-quarter production of 4,774 vehicles and deliveries of 3,953 units— marking a modest year-over-year increase but short of analyst expectations amid slower-than-hoped demand for the new Gravity SUV. Financially, Lucid continues to face steep losses and negative gross margins despite revenue growth. The company is currently attempting to ramp up growth under the leadership of CEO Silvio Napoli, who assumed the role in June. Napoli undertook a leadership overhaul recently and replaced CFO Taoufiq Boussaid with automotive finance veteran Alexander De Bock. He also appointed new executives for technology, customer, digital, and transformation roles, flattened the reporting structure by halving direct reports to the CEO, and eliminated the COO position. These moves followed June layoffs of roughly 1,500 employees, about 18% of the workforce, and the removal of a second production shift at the Arizona plant, aimed at delivering roughly $158 million in annual savings. The company has relied heavily on its PIF for support through it all. In late April 2026, Ayar purchased $550 million of Lucid’s Series C convertible preferred stock and expanded Lucid’s delayed-draw term loan facility by $500 million. Most recently, on July 6, Lucid drew $800 million under those existing facilities, converting committed credit into immediate cash. On November 11, 2024, UnitedHealth Group (NYSE:UNH | UNH Price Prediction) traded at $596.08. By May 30, 2025, it had fallen to $290.17, a 51.32% decline on a dividend-adjusted basis. From that bottom through October 15, 2026, the stock rose 40.64%. A delayed intraday quote on October 15, 2026, put it at $408.08, still below the November 2024 peak. If you own SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (NYSEARCA:DIA), UnitedHealth’s share of your fund shrank and swelled along that entire path, driven solely by its share price. State Street Global Advisors describes DIA’s benchmark as a price-weighted index of 30 component common stocks. Price-weighted means one simple rule: the higher a stock’s share price, the bigger its slice of the fund. Company size, earnings, and business quality play no role. As UnitedHealth’s share price fell by half, its influence inside DIA fell with it. As the price climbed back, that influence returned automatically. The fund holds the most of a stock when it is most expensive and the least when it is cheapest. Those shifts come from the weighting rule alone. The relationship above follows directly from the published weighting method. State Street Global Advisors reports UnitedHealth at 4.55% of DIA as of October 14, 2026, making it the fund’s fifth-largest holding. State Street Global Advisors lists Goldman Sachs (NYSE:GS) as the largest position at 10.11% on the same date. Caterpillar (NYSE:CAT) ranks second at 8.62% and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) third at 6.14%.  The fourth-largest holding sits at 4.90%. Goldman leads because, under price weighting, the top position is by definition the highest-priced stock. That ranking reflects what one share costs. Price weighting instead follows the number printed on a single share, a number a stock split can cut overnight with no change to the underlying company. The University of New Hampshire welcomed 3,000 new students to its Durham and Manchester campuses this fall, representing a nearly 5 percent increase from last year’s incoming class. The university said the uptick in new students is bucking national trends. First-year undergraduate students at UNH increased 3.5 percent and transfer students increased 11.2 percent, compared with 2025 enrollment numbers. Other numbers from UNH about this fall’s new class: Incoming students posted an average high school GPA of 3.7 UNH awarded a record $40 million in financial aid to incoming students, with 96 percent of incoming students receiving aid. Out-of-state enrollment grew 11 percent, while in-state enrollment grew 1.7 percent. UNH said these figures reflect its “strengthened position in the New Hampshire market.” “While there are many challenges facing higher education right now, by focusing on a high-quality academic experience, experiential learning, and creating value for students and their families, we are increasingly a first-choice for many,” UNH President Elizabeth Chilton said in a news release Tuesday. Earlier this month, the University System of New Hampshire announced it would begin offering free tuition at the state’s public colleges to certain students beginning next year. Eligible students must be New Hampshire residents, meet certain academic requirements and be attending one of the schools for the first time. Their families cannot earn more than $100,000 a year. A UNH spokesperson estimated the change in eligibility requirements will mean an additional 29 percent of next year’s incoming class will qualify for the program. UnitedHealth Group Incorporated UNH is refining its Medicare Advantage strategy, emphasizing high-value health maintenance organization (HMO) plans and specialized coverage for seniors with complex healthcare needs. For 2027, UnitedHealthcare plans to prioritize Chronic Special Needs Plans (C-SNPs) and Dual Eligible Special Needs Plans (D-SNPs). The opportunity is substantial. UnitedHealthcare's C-SNPs will be available to nearly 50 million Medicare-eligible individuals in 2027, offering tailored support for people managing conditions such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease and chronic heart failure. Meanwhile, its D-SNPs will reach approximately 74% of dual-eligible individuals, facilitating coordinated Medicare and Medicaid benefits. These plans can connect members with more coordinated care, medication support and preventive services, potentially creating opportunities to improve outcomes and limit avoidable healthcare spending. UNH's approach also fits its broader shift toward more selective Medicare Advantage offerings. The company is adjusting plan benefits and market participation to better align coverage with healthcare costs. It expects Medicare margins to approach the upper end of its 2%-4% target range in 2026, reflecting improved cost management and product positioning. Integrated care through Optum Health could further support this strategy by coordinating services for members with complex needs. Star ratings remain another consideration. UnitedHealthcare reported that at least 69% of its Medicare Advantage members are in plans rated four stars or higher for 2027. UNH's focus on special needs plans could support targeted growth, but execution, medical costs and quality performance can shape the results. Some of UNH's major competitors in the healthcare service provider space are Humana Inc. HUM and Centene Corporation CNC. Humana is expanding its Chronic Condition Special Needs Plans into Pennsylvania, Utah and Wisconsin for 2027. HUM's focus on tailored coverage and coordinated care could attract beneficiaries with complex conditions, while stronger Star Ratings may support its Medicare Advantage competitiveness. Through its Wellcare brand, Centene is emphasizing affordable Medicare Advantage coverage and integrated care for dual-eligible beneficiaries in 2027. CNC's coordinated Medicare-Medicaid offerings could strengthen its appeal among members with complex needs, although managing medical expenses remains key.                         Kirsteen Mackay UnitedHealth raised its 2026 earnings outlook to at least $20.50 per adjusted share as third quarter results showed a lower medical care ratio and more profit. UnitedHealth's third quarter showed its cost controls are taking hold, as a lower medical care ratio helped lift operating earnings and supported a higher 2026 outlook. Gains came across UnitedHealthcare and Optum despite falling membership. Management sees 2027 growth near the low end of its long-term target, though medical costs, Medicaid funding and federal legal actions remain risks. UnitedHealth Group Inc. (NYSE: UNH) on October 13, 2026, raised its full year 2026 earnings outlook and now expects adjusted net earnings of at least $20.50 per share. The company said the forecast incorporates its experience through the third quarter 2026. On a GAAP basis, UnitedHealth now expects full year earnings of at least $19.50 per share. GAAP refers to standard US accounting rules, while the adjusted figure excludes items such as the amortization of acquired intangible assets and gains or losses tied to business sales. The updated outlook follows third quarter adjusted earnings of $4.69 per share, compared with $2.92 in the third quarter 2025. GAAP diluted earnings were $4.56 per share, up from $2.59 a year earlier. The release lists the Department of Justice's legal actions concerning UnitedHealth's participation in the Medicare program among the factors that could cause results to differ from expectations. It also cites changes in Medicare, the CMS star ratings program and risk adjustment data validation audits, which review the diagnosis data used to set government payments. UnitedHealth's medical care ratio, the share of premium revenue spent on patient care, was 88.4% in the third quarter, compared with 89.9% a year earlier. The company attributed the decline to medical cost management, benefit design changes and pricing. The ratio included $610 million of net favorable prior period reserve development related to 2026 dates of service. This means UnitedHealth's earlier estimates of claims owed for care delivered this year proved higher than the amounts now expected. Earnings from operations were $6.6 billion, compared with $4.3 billion in the third quarter 2025. The company said the increase was driven by execution across both its UnitedHealthcare insurance unit and its Optum health services unit. Consolidated revenue was $112.7 billion, compared with $113.2 billion a year earlier. Revenue in the second quarter 2026 was $112 billion. The operating cost ratio, which measures administrative costs against revenue, was 12.8%, compared with 13.5% in the third quarter 2025. The company said efficiency gains were partly offset by increased spending on technology, processes and staff. "Our third quarter results reflect the discipline and execution our teams are bringing to every part of our business," Stephen Hemsley, Chief Executive Officer, UnitedHealth Group, said in the earnings release. UnitedHealthcare earned $2.8 billion from operations in the quarter, up from $1.8 billion a year earlier, on revenue of $86.3 billion. The unit served 48.3 million people, compared with about 50.1 million at the end of the third quarter 2025. The number of seniors served through Medicare Advantage, including programs for complex populations also covered by Medicaid, has contracted by 935,000 since year-end 2025, according to the release. Optum Health revenue fell 10% to $22.9 billion. The company said it served fewer patients under value-based care, arrangements in which providers are paid based on patient outcomes and costs, in markets where it lacked enough presence to sustain its clinicians. Optum Health earnings from operations rose to $735 million from $41 million a year earlier. The company attributed the change to operational discipline and medical cost management in its value-based care markets. Optum Rx, the company's pharmacy benefits business, reported earnings from operations of $1.7 billion, compared with $1.5 billion a year earlier. Adjusted scripts fell to 393 million from 414 million, which the company linked to membership declines at UnitedHealthcare and other customers. Optum Insight, the data and technology unit, reported revenue of $5.5 billion, up 3% from a year earlier. Its earnings from operations rose to $1.3 billion from $920 million. On the earnings call, Tim Noel, who leads UnitedHealthcare, said commercial medical cost trends are running above the company's initial expectation of 11%. He cited costs tied to the No Surprises Act dispute process, greater cost intensity from clinicians and high-cost specialty drugs. The No Surprises Act is a federal law intended to protect patients from unexpected medical bills. Noel said arbitration awards under its dispute process can approach nearly 6% of total medical spending in some regions. Noel said UnitedHealth continues to view 2026 as a trough year for core Medicaid margins, which it now expects to be moderately better than negative 1%. He said the main variable remains the timing and adequacy of state funding. UnitedHealth's debt-to-capital ratio was 41.7% as of September 30, 2026, compared with 41.2% at the end of the second quarter. The company said it continues to target approximately 40% by year-end. The company repurchased $5 billion of its stock and paid $6.2 billion in dividends through the first nine months of 2026. Chief Financial Officer Wayne DeVeydt said the company expects dividends to exceed $8 billion by year-end. Management said it views the lower end of its 13% to 16% long-term growth target as a more reasonable starting point for 2027 and plans a fuller update in December, though elevated medical cost trends, government program funding and the Department of Justice's legal actions remain key risks to that outlook.
